strategy_title: Capping Registers via maxnreg Causes Severe Spill Regression
strategy_description: Adding maxnreg=128 to Triton configs successfully doubled theoretical occupancy (12.5%→25%) and halved registers/thread (255→128), but caused a 3.25x slowdown. The no-eligible-warp fraction worsened from 62% to 84%, warp cycles per issued instruction jumped from 5.26 to 24.88, and DRAM throughput rose from 17% to 47% — indicating that the compiler aggressively spilled register-resident accumulator values to local memory (DRAM), generating ~6x more L2 traffic (524M→2990M sectors). The occupancy gain was completely overwhelmed by the spill traffic: when the accumulator tile is large (e.g. 128×128 FP32 = 16,384 values), capping registers forces massive spilling that is far more costly than the latency-hiding benefit of extra warps.
applicable_when: Never applicable when the accumulator tile is large (BLOCK_M * BLOCK_N > ~4096 FP32 values). The spill traffic from capping registers on a large accumulator always exceeds the occupancy benefit.
do_not_apply_when: When the accumulator tile is large (e.g. BLOCK_M=128, BLOCK_N=128 → 16,384 FP32 values). Capping registers forces the compiler to spill accumulator values to local memory (DRAM), causing DRAM throughput to spike (17%→47%), warp stall cycles to increase 5x (5.26→24.88 cycles/instruction), and total executed instructions to grow 39% (5.0B→7.0B). The net result is a 3.25x slowdown despite doubling occupancy. Only consider maxnreg if the accumulator fits comfortably within the capped register budget.
framework_notes: Triton-specific: maxnreg parameter in triton.Config caps the register file per thread. The Triton compiler will spill excess live values (especially large accumulator tiles) to local memory. CUDA equivalent: __launch_bounds__(block_size, min_blocks_per_sm) has the same spill risk when the register budget is insufficient for the live value set.
